summary: An informational memo describing the architecture of the CCSO Nameserver (Ph), a database service from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign used by many organizations to look up people and other things.

eli5.summary: An online phone book system that many schools and offices used to look up people.

questions: how do you query the ph directory
subtitle: A directory service protocol for querying and managing a database of people and information.

tldr.problem: Organizations needed a simple way to look up information about people (phone numbers, email addresses) and other things in a searchable database accessible over the internet.
tldr.mechanism: Ph is a client-server protocol on TCP port 105 that defines a command language for querying, adding, changing, and deleting entries in a structured database with named fields, supporting multiple field types, access control, and various authentication methods.
tldr.outcome: Ph was widely adopted by universities and organizations as their choice for publicly available people directories, though it has since been superseded by modern directory services.

today: RFC 2378 is an Informational document describing the Ph nameserver protocol as deployed by CCSO at the University of Illinois. Ph was widely adopted by universities and organizations for directory services throughout the 1990s, serving as the canonical people-lookup service for many institutions. However, it has been largely superseded by modern directory services such as LDAP and web-based directory systems. The protocol remains documented in this RFC for historical reference and for any organizations that still operate Ph servers.

sections.title: What Ph Is
sections.content:
The Ph Nameserver from the Computing and Communications Services Office (CCSO) at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign is designed to be a simple, scalable directory service. At its simplest, Ph is a computer-resident phone book that can be queried over the internet. However, it can hold arbitrary information about people, organizations, or other entities in a structured form with named fields and return information in response to queries.

Ph was designed to keep a relatively small amount of information about a relatively large number of entries and provide internet access to that information. The database manager decides which views (collections of fields) to present for each object type. Each field has a field descriptor that defines the field's maximum length, properties (keywords), and a description of what kind of information it should hold.

Ph is local in scope: each server maintains its own database and does not refer clients to other servers. However, servers may contain references to other Ph servers that clients can use to query other directory services.
sections.eli5: Ph is a database of people or things with a simple query language. You ask for someone by name, and the server tells you their phone number, email, or other information. Each server has its own database, and you cannot ask one server about data on another server, but servers can tell you how to find other servers.

sections.title: Fields and Information Model
sections.content:
Ph organizes information into fields. Each field has a name, a maximum length, and a set of keywords that describe its properties. A single field descriptor for the entire database defines these properties.

Keywords control field behavior: Always forces a field to be included in every result; Indexed marks fields kept in the database's index for efficient lookups (at least one indexed field must be in every query); Lookup allows a field to be used in queries; Public allows anyone to view the field; Private restricts viewing to database administrators (called Heros); Change allows the entry's owner to modify it; Unique rejects changes that would duplicate another entry's value; Encrypt requires the value to be encrypted before transmission; Default causes the field to be returned if no explicit return clause is given.

Ph supports two main character sets: US-ASCII (the default, restricted to printable characters) and ISO-8859-1 (allowing 8-bit characters). When 8-bit characters must be displayed in ASCII, the server uses Quoted-Printable encoding.
sections.eli5: Each piece of information (like a phone number or email) is a field. Each field has rules: some fields are searchable, some are public, some can be changed by the owner, some must be unique, and some must be encrypted. These rules control how the field behaves.

sections.title: Client-Server Communication
sections.content:
Ph uses a simple text-based protocol over TCP port 105. Clients send commands consisting of a keyword optionally followed by values, separated by spaces or tabs, terminated by CRLF. Servers respond with result codes (numeric) optionally followed by entry indices, field names, and text.

Result codes follow a pattern similar to FTP: leading digit 1 means in progress, 2 means success, 3 means more information needed, 4 means temporary failure, 5 means permanent failure, 6 means Ph-specific codes. Multi-line responses use negated codes for continuation lines (e.g., -200) and terminate with the positive code.

Commands are case-insensitive for keywords but case-sensitive for values. To support values with spaces, double quotes can be used, with backslash escaping for quotes, newlines, and backslashes.
sections.eli5: The client sends typed commands like 'query name=smith return email phone' and the server sends back numbered responses with the information, one line per field. If there are many results, the server uses - signs to show continuation lines and a final number to mark the end.

sections.title: Query and Management Commands
sections.content:
query is the primary command for searching. It takes a selection clause (field=value pairs, defaulting to 'name' if no field is specified) and an optional return clause specifying which fields to return. Matching is word-by-word and case-insensitive by default; exact phrase matching uses double quotes. Wildcards include '*' (zero or more characters), '+' (one or more), and '?' (exactly one).

Other commands allow authenticated users to modify the database: add creates new entries, change modifies fields in existing entries, and delete removes entries. All of these require login. login initiates authentication with a challenge-response mechanism using three-rotor Enigma encryption, or optionally with Kerberos v4/v5, GSS-API, or clear-text passwords.

Administrative commands include status (shows server message and status), siteinfo (returns server configuration), fields (lists available fields), set (configures session options), and help (retrieves help text).
sections.eli5: You can query the database by typing what you're looking for and what fields you want back. If you log in, you can add new people, change existing information, or delete entries. The server has special commands to show you what fields exist and how to configure your session.

sections.title: Authentication and Access Control
sections.content:
Ph defines multiple authentication methods that a server can support, ordered by site preference: automatic login, interactive login, ANSI X9.9 token devices, Kerberos v4, Kerberos v5, GSS-API, email-based authentication, encrypted password response to challenge, clear-text password, and HMAC with SHA-1.

The email authentication method is a weak form suitable for convenient access: it accepts the connection origin port, the client's canonical hostname, and the local user ID to confirm the user's identity. Heroes are administrative users who can view restricted fields and change any entry in the database; their privileges are controlled by an access control list (acl) field.

The document notes significant security limitations: without encryption or mutual authentication mechanisms like Kerberos, all traffic can be sniffed by machines on the network, and clear-text traffic can be modified in transit. Suggestions for improvement include TLS and IPSec.
sections.eli5: You log in to modify entries. The server can use various ways to check your identity, from simple email-based checks to strong encryption methods. Heros are superusers who can see private information and change anything.
